newsitem.title: EGYPT: Slow Mideast peace snags region's mega-projects.
newsitem.headline: Slow Mideast peace snags region's mega-projects.

text.p: Middle East peace snags will hold up key regional megaprojects at a Cairo economic meeting next week and analysts say they may stay on the drawing board unless there is progress in Israel's negotiations with its Arab neighbours.

"When there is peace, there will be progress. Otherwise it's difficult to imagine it happening," said Ahmed Abu el-Kheir, Egypt's foreign ministry coordinator for the Middle East and North Africa Economic Conference.
Chances for a quick peace settlement between Israel and its Arab neighbours have dimmed considerably since the Jewish state voted in right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Netanyahu refuses to exchange Arab lands for peace, the main principle of a deal Israel approved at a 1991 peace conference.

He is also trying to renegotiate parts of an agreement with the Palestinians to secure Jewish settlers living in the West Bank town of Hebron, the last of seven towns Israel was supposed to give back to Palestinian self-rule.
Economic analysts privately admit it is difficult to see key regional projects advancing without progress in Israeli peace talks with Lebanon and Syria.
Here are the main Middle Eastern projects at stake:
REGIONAL POWER GRID
Since they approved the plans in April, Arab countries have been priming their electricity grids for incorporation into a huge regional network expected to be running by 1999.

The multimillion dollar project will be funded entirely by the Arab Fund for Economic and Social Development and sees countries from Morocco to the west and Iraq to the east sharing their power. Turkey is also interested in joining the grid.
But Israel has so far been skipped from the master plan. Economists hope the Jewish state will have made peace with Syria, Lebanon and the Palestinians by the time it is finalised.

The Gulf states are still trying to finish the initial phase of the project and link up their grids. Egypt and Jordan are currently laying a cable under the Gulf of Aqaba and onto the Palestinian self-rule territories.
MIDDLE EAST DEVELOPMENT BANK
The United States proposed the Middle East Development Bank in 1994 during the first Middle East and North Africa conference in Casablanca and it was ratified a year later.

The bank aims at financing regional projects in a post-peace Middle East and according to Raouf Saad, an Egyptian assistant foreign minister, the institution is waiting only for approval by the U.S. Congress.

"The agreement of the bank has been finalised and has been deposited with the United Nations since August 28 and is open for signature by the 19 founding members as well as any new members," Saad told the state-owned newspaper al-Ahram Weekly.

The administration needs congressional approval to finance a hefty 21 percent of the bank's capital -- $52 million annually for five years. Saad said the Clinton administration was determined to pay its share.
"If the U.S. doesn't sign, it would weaken the credibility of the bank to start without a large shareholder. We expect the bank to come into operation by November 1997," he added.
REGIONAL BUSINESS COUNCIL
The council was designed to promote private-sector trade and investment in the Middle East but progress beyond the drawing board has been hampered by slow progress on the peace process.

The steering committee of the council -- made up of Egypt, Jordan, Israel and the Palestinians -- has yet to meet as Palestinian businessmen say they cannot talk shop while Israel continues to "strangle" their economy.
"The (council) has highlighted how a delay in the peace process could negatively affect cooperation," Saad said.

The businessmen say that local industries and businesses have suffered from closures imposed regularly on the West Bank and Gaza Strip since 1994. The closures have also reduced per capita income by 35 percent.

"We've been ready to take part in many preparatory meetings but one country or another doesn't make it," said Said el-Tawil, chairman of the Egyptian Businessmen's Association. "The political atmosphere is just not ideal."
REGIONAL GAS PIPELINE - "THE PEACE PIPELINE"

Political differences over the peace process have not derailed long-term Egyptian plans to supply natural gas to Israel but Egypt has said it hopes for a better political atmosphere by the time the deal is finally done.

The project, dubbed the "Peace Pipeline" by the United States, involves building a pipeline from gas fields in Egypt's Delta region to Israel and from there to the Palestinian self-rule areas and then on to Jordan. There are negotiations to have it stretch all the way to Turkey.
Egyptian Oil Minister Hamdi el-Banbi said technical talks continued on the proposed deal, which envisages Israel buying two billion cubic metres of gas annually from the year 2000.

He also said Egyptian working groups were drafting an initial agreement while Israel has an international company to study gas pipeline routes and establish a master plan for gas utilisation in the Jewish state.
FREE TRADE AGREEMENTS
In May, Egypt and Jordan signed a free trade accord to boost joint ventures in the private sector and to gain greater market access to the world's trade blocs.
Both countries hope the deal is a precursor to a much-touted -- but little realised -- Arab free trade zone.
Egypt has repeatedly called for a unified economic bloc similar to the 15-nation European Union to strengthen the region's competitive power but inter-Arab deals are limited.
But Arab countries have signed trade accords with the Europeans and many have also ratified the World Trade Organisation agreement to stimulate trade.
The eight Mediterranean Arab states and Israel are negotiating the EuroMed treaty, which aims at transforming the region into a free trade zone.

But delegates at a May meeting of the REDWIG (Regional Economic Development Working Group) have said Israel's over-zealous security checks on its borders were a major impediment to regional cooperation.
REGIONAL TRANSPORT PROJECTS

Many of the regional projects remain in the identification and feasibility phase but REDWIG, which is part of the multilateral Middle East peace talks launched in 1991, has said that the transport sector has seen most progress.
It identified 13 projects that are just waiting for the $278.40 million needed to fund them to get going.
They include the $22.8 million rehabilition of the Allenby Bridge across the Jordan Valley to facilitate Jordan's trade with the Palestinians, already secure with Japanese aid.
Others in the planning stage are a $22 million Mediterranean Coastal Railway, a $40 million Sinai-Gaza highway, a $30 million Haifa-Irbid road, and a $34 million Gaza-Israel rail link.
RED SEA AND MEDITERRANEAN DEVELOPMENT PROJECTS
Palestinian-Israeli violence sparked by Netanyahu's policies has sent jitters throughout the world and put a damper on the region's most lucrative industry: tourism.

The Arab world gets only two percent of the world's annual $370 billion tourism spending, says the Arab Hotels and Tourism Union, even though it boasts extraordinary attractions from Egypt's Pyramids to Jordan's rose-red city of Petra.
But foreigners tend to lump the region into one and have been staying away.
Intraregional groupings like the Middle East Mediterranean Travel and Tourism Association is also snagged on the lack of progress in the peace process.
Saad has said the association will be finalised after regional partners approved its charter. Analysts say that this may be delayed and initial meetings do not bode well.

Egyptian and Palestinian delegates boycotted the last meeting which took place during last month's bloody clashes in the self-rule areas, sparked by Netanyahu's decision to open a tunnel near Islam's holiest shrine.

But all is not lost, Saad said. In the Cairo summit, Egypt will discuss a project to develop the area of Taba, Eilat and Aqaba on the Red Sea and another scheme to turn the southeast Mediterranean into a Riviera-type zone.
